chunks.text: # Basics Of Linear And Logistic Regression Learn everything about basics of Linear and Logistic regression end to end Linear & Logistic Regression — Complete End-to-End Guide This project provides a structured, end-to-end implementation of Linear Regression and Logistic Regression using Scikit-Learn Pipelines. The goal is not just to run models, but to deeply understand: The theory behind each algorithm Proper preprocessing techniques Safe train-test separation Model evaluation metrics Avoiding data leakage Interpreting results correctly These models form the foundation of Machine Learning. Mastering them makes advanced models much easier to understand. Overview This project contains two notebooks: Notebook Task Target Variable Model basiclinearregression.ipynb Regression SalePrice (continuous) LinearRegression() basiclogisticregression.ipynb Binary Classification HighPrice (0 or 1) LogisticRegression(maxiter=2000)

chunks.title: Basics Of Linear And Logistic Regression
chunks.text: sion SalePrice (continuous) LinearRegression() basiclogisticregression.ipynb Binary Classification HighPrice (0 or 1) LogisticRegression(maxiter=2000) Both notebooks demonstrate: Clean ML workflow using Pipeline Separate preprocessing for numeric and categorical features Proper train-test splitting before any preprocessing is applied Evaluation using metrics appropriate to the task Visualization of performance (logistic regression notebook) Probability-based interpretation of classifiers (logistic regression notebook) All transformations are handled safely using Scikit-Learn's Pipeline and ColumnTransformer. Dataset: House Prices – Advanced Regression Techniques This project uses the House Prices – Advanced Regression Techniques dataset from Kaggle. Dataset link: The dataset contains residential home sales data from Ames, Iowa. It is designed to challenge participants to predict house sale prices using a wide range of explanatory variables.

chunks.title: Basics Of Linear And Logistic Regression
chunks.text: al home sales data from Ames, Iowa. It is designed to challenge participants to predict house sale prices using a wide range of explanatory variables. The original target variable is: SalePrice — the final sale price of the house (continuous variable). Dataset Characteristics 1,460 training examples 80 features (37 numeric + 43 categorical, before removing the target) Mix of: Numerical variables (e.g., LotArea, YearBuilt, GrLivArea, GarageArea) Categorical variables (e.g., Neighborhood, HouseStyle, ExterQual, Foundation) Contains missing values throughout — requires imputation before modeling Requires encoding of categorical variables before modeling Why This Dataset? This dataset is ideal for learning because it: Includes both numeric and categorical features, requiring a real preprocessing pipeline Has missing values that must be handled thoughtfully (different strategies for different column types) Can be used for both regression (predicting SalePrice) and classification (e.g., above/below median) Is widely used in ML education and competitions, making it easy to compare results Using SalePrice for Logistic Regression

chunks.text: (e.g., above/below median) Is widely used in ML education and competitions, making it easy to compare results Using SalePrice for Logistic Regression The original dataset is designed for regression, where SalePrice is a continuous target. However, Logistic Regression requires a binary classification target. To adapt the dataset for classification, the logistic regression notebook transforms SalePrice into a binary label: Step 1 — Compute the Median Sale Price The median value of SalePrice is computed across the full dataset. The median acts as a threshold to split houses into two groups. Step 2 — Create a Binary Target Variable A new column is created: This converts the continuous regression problem into a binary classification problem. What This Means Instead of predicting the exact sale price, the model answers: "Is this house priced above the median?" Why Use the Median? It creates a naturally balanced split between classes (50% positive, 50% negative) It avoids bias introduced by extreme outlier prices It makes the threshold intuitive and interpretable Linear Regression What is Linear Regression?

chunks.title: Basics Of Linear And Logistic Regression
chunks.text: e) It avoids bias introduced by extreme outlier prices It makes the threshold intuitive and interpretable Linear Regression What is Linear Regression? Linear Regression is a supervised learning algorithm used to predict continuous values. In this project it predicts SalePrice — the final sale price of a house in dollars. It assumes a linear relationship between the input features and the target variable, modeled by: Where: y = predicted house price x₁, x₂, ..., xₙ = input features β₀ = intercept β₁, ..., βₙ = learned coefficients (one per feature) Each coefficient represents how much the target changes for a one-unit change in the corresponding feature, holding all others constant. How the Model Learns — OLS Linear Regression uses Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) to find the best-fitting line by minimizing the Sum of Squared Errors (SSE): Squaring the errors: Prevents positive and negative errors from canceling each other out Penalizes larger errors more heavily than small ones Key Assumptions

chunks.title: Basics Of Linear And Logistic Regression
chunks.text: g the errors: Prevents positive and negative errors from canceling each other out Penalizes larger errors more heavily than small ones Key Assumptions 1. Linearity — The relationship between features and target is linear 2. Independence — Observations are independent of each other 3. Homoscedasticity — Residuals have constant variance across all predictions 4. No perfect multicollinearity — Features should not be exact linear combinations of each other 5. Normality of residuals — Important for statistical inference and confidence intervals Why Preprocessing Is Critical Linear Regression is sensitive to: Missing values — The algorithm cannot handle NaN inputs Feature scale — Features on very different scales can distort coefficient magnitudes Multicollinearity — Correlated features can make coefficients unstable Non-numeric features — Categorical variables must be encoded before the model can use them Linear Regression Workflow (Step-by-Step)

Fit on training data — linregpipeline.fit(Xtrain, ytrain) 9. Predict on test data — linregpipeline.predict(Xtest) 10. Evaluate — R² and RMSE Linear Regression Evaluation Metrics R² (Coefficient of Determination)

chunks.text: Predict on test data — linregpipeline.predict(Xtest) 10. Evaluate — R² and RMSE Linear Regression Evaluation Metrics R² (Coefficient of Determination) Measures the proportion of variance in the target that is explained by the model. Range: 0 to 1 1.0 → model explains all variance (perfect fit) 0.0 → model explains none of the variance (no better than predicting the mean) Result on this dataset: R² = 0.686 This means the model explains 68.6% of the variance in house sale prices. RMSE (Root Mean Squared Error) Measures average prediction error in the same unit as the target variable (dollars) Lower is better Penalizes large errors more than small ones Result on this dataset: RMSE = $49,047 On average, the model's predicted sale price is off by approximately $49,047. Logistic Regression What is Logistic Regression? Logistic Regression is a supervised learning algorithm used for binary classification. Instead of predicting a continuous value, it predicts the probability that an observation belongs to class 1. In this project it predicts HighPrice — whether a house's sale price is above the median. The Sigmoid Function

Evaluate — Log Loss Data Preprocessing Why Preprocessing Is Important Raw data cannot be fed directly into machine learning models: Models cannot handle missing values (NaN) All features must be numeric; categorical variables must be encoded Feature scaling prevents large-magnitude features from dominating Preprocessing must be learned from training data only — applying it to the full dataset before splitting causes data leakage Numeric Pipeline Applied to all numeric columns (37 features): 1. SimpleImputer(strategy="median") — Fills missing values with the median. Median is preferred over mean because it is robust to outliers. 2. StandardScaler() — Standardizes each feature to have mean = 0 and standard deviation = 1. Required because Linear and Logistic Regression are both sensitive to feature scale. Categorical Pipeline Applied to all categorical (object-type) columns (43 features):

chunks.title: Basics Of Linear And Logistic Regression
chunks.text: near and Logistic Regression are both sensitive to feature scale. Categorical Pipeline Applied to all categorical (object-type) columns (43 features): 1. SimpleImputer(strategy="mostfrequent") — Fills missing values with the most frequent category in that column. 2. OneHotEncoder(drop="first", handleunknown="ignore") Converts each category into a set of binary columns drop="first" drops the first dummy column per feature to avoid multicollinearity (the dummy variable trap) handleunknown="ignore" encodes unseen categories in the test set as all zeros instead of raising an error ColumnTransformer ColumnTransformer applies different pipelines to different column types simultaneously: Numeric columns → numeric pipeline Categorical columns → categorical pipeline remainder="drop" discards any columns not explicitly specified Train-Test Split Data is split before any preprocessing is applied: 80% Training set — used to fit the model and all preprocessing transformers 20% Test set — used only for final evaluation This gives a test set of 292 samples (from 1,460 total). For regression (linear): standard split, no stratification needed.

chunks.title: Basics Of Linear And Logistic Regression
chunks.text: only for final evaluation This gives a test set of 292 samples (from 1,460 total). For regression (linear): standard split, no stratification needed. For classification (logistic): stratified split (stratify=yclf) ensures both training and test sets maintain the same proportion of class 0 and class 1 labels. Why Split Before Preprocessing? Fitting preprocessing (e.g., computing the median, learning categories) on the full dataset and then splitting would leak information about the test set into the training process. This inflates performance metrics and creates a model that would perform worse on truly new data. Using Pipeline, the preprocessor is: Fit only on Xtrain during .fit() Applied (transform only) to Xtest during .predict() This guarantees no data leakage. Classification Evaluation Metrics The logistic regression notebook evaluates the model using six distinct methods: 1. Accuracy Measures the overall fraction of correct predictions. Reliable when classes are balanced. Result: 90.4% 2. Confusion Matrix Breaks predictions into four categories: Predicted 0 Predicted 1

chunks.title: Basics Of Linear And Logistic Regression
chunks.text: ct predictions. Reliable when classes are balanced. Result: 90.4% 2. Confusion Matrix Breaks predictions into four categories: Predicted 0 Predicted 1 Actual 0 True Negative (TN) = 132 False Positive (FP) = 14 Actual 1 False Negative (FN) = 14 True Positive (TP) = 132 True Positive (TP): Correctly predicted as high price True Negative (TN): Correctly predicted as not high price False Positive (FP): Predicted high price but was not (Type I error) False Negative (FN): Predicted not high price but was (Type II error) The confusion matrix is plotted using ConfusionMatrixDisplay from Scikit-Learn. 3. Precision Out of all predicted positives, how many were actually positive? Result: 0.904 4. Recall Out of all actual positives, how many did the model correctly identify? Result: 0.904 5. F1 Score The harmonic mean of precision and recall. Balances both metrics and is useful when the cost of false positives and false negatives differs. Result: 0.904 6. ROC Curve & AUC The ROC (Receiver Operating Characteristic) Curve plots: False Positive Rate (FPR) on the x-axis True Positive Rate (TPR) on the y-axis ...across all possible classification thresholds from 0 to 1.

chunks.title: Basics Of Linear And Logistic Regression
chunks.text: ve plots: False Positive Rate (FPR) on the x-axis True Positive Rate (TPR) on the y-axis ...across all possible classification thresholds from 0 to 1. AUC (Area Under the Curve) summarizes the ROC curve as a single number: 1.0 → perfect classifier 0.5 → no better than random guessing AUC represents the probability that the model ranks a random positive example higher than a random negative example. Result: ROC-AUC = 0.972 The ROC curve is plotted using matplotlib. 7. Log Loss Measures how well-calibrated the predicted probabilities are. Lower log loss means the model produces more confident and correct probability estimates. Logistic Regression directly minimizes log loss during training. Result: Log Loss = 0.229 Pipeline Architecture Using Scikit-Learn Pipeline bundles preprocessing and the model into a single object, ensuring: No manual transformation of test data No risk of applying the wrong transformation parameters Reproducible, production-ready workflows Prevention of data leakage Pipeline Flow: Results Summary Linear Regression Metric Value R² 0.686 RMSE $49,047

Does This Apply Only to Linear and Logistic Regression? No. The preprocessing techniques shown here apply broadly to: Ridge / Lasso Regression Support Vector Machines K-Nearest Neighbors Neural Networks Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, XGBoost Only minor adjustments are needed depending on the algorithm. For example, tree-based models are less sensitive to feature scaling, but imputation, encoding, and leakage prevention apply universally.

Key Principles Reinforced Throughout Always split data before fitting any transformer Never fit preprocessing on the full dataset or the test set Handle missing values before scaling Encode categorical features before modeling Apply SMOTE only on training data Use Pipelines to keep preprocessing consistent and leakage-free Save full pipelines — not just models — for deployment Final Takeaway Data preprocessing is not a minor step — it is foundational. A model is only as good as the data it is trained on. Well-structured preprocessing improves model performance, prevents leakage, ensures reproducibility, and makes the entire workflow production-ready. Mastering preprocessing is one of the highest-leverage skills in machine learning.

chunks.text: # LLM Research Scraper Simple to complex projects implemented using LLMs Research Paper Summarizer A tool that fetches any research paper and generates a structured, plain-English summary using Claude (Anthropic). Instead of reading a dense 20-page academic paper, you give it a paper ID and get back a clean breakdown of what the paper is about, what problem it solves, what they found, and why it matters. Built on top of concepts from Week 1 / Day 1 of the LLM Engineering course by Ed Donner. What Problem Does This Solve? Research papers are written for other researchers. They are dense, jargon-heavy, and time-consuming to read. This tool fetches the paper's metadata and abstract from a free API and feeds it to Claude, which then produces a structured summary in plain English — so anyone can understand what a paper is about without reading the whole thing. Why Not Just Scrape the Website? The original project used requests + BeautifulSoup to scrape websites. The problem with research sites like ResearchGate or Google Scholar is that they actively block bots — you get 403 errors or security checkpoints instead of the paper content.

chunks.title: LLM Research Scraper
chunks.text: sites like ResearchGate or Google Scholar is that they actively block bots — you get 403 errors or security checkpoints instead of the paper content. The solution here is to skip scraping entirely and use free, official APIs that are designed to be accessed programmatically. No bot detection. No errors. Clean structured data every time. Data Sources This project supports two sources. You can use either one depending on where the paper is published. arXiv A free, open repository of research papers in AI, ML, Computer Science, Math, Physics, and more Where most AI/ML papers are published first — including the original Transformer paper and GPT papers Provides: title, authors, abstract, subject categories No API key required Returns data in XML format Semantic Scholar A free academic search engine built by the Allen Institute for AI Indexes over 200 million papers across all fields — not just CS/ML Useful for papers in medicine, biology, economics, and anything not on arXiv Provides: title, authors, abstract, year, citation count, fields of study No API key required for basic usage (100 requests per 5 minutes) Returns data in JSON format What Claude Extracts From Each Paper

What is this paper about? — A plain-English explanation of the topic 2. The problem they are solving — What gap or challenge does this research address 3. Their approach — How the authors tackled the problem 4. Key findings — What they discovered or proved 5. Why it matters — The real-world impact or significance 6. Limitations and future directions — What the paper doesn't cover and what comes next 7. Who should read this? — What kind of person or professional would benefit most How It Works Project Structure All code is in one notebook to keep things simple and self-contained. chunks.text: # Open Source LLMs Api Wrapper Using an API wrapper where the user selects an open source LLM model without changing any code. Contract Review Tool — Multi-Provider API Wrapper A tool that reads a contract (PDF or text file) and uses an AI model to extract all the important key points — so you don't have to read the whole thing yourself. The tool supports multiple AI providers (Groq, Google Gemini, OpenAI, Mistral, and local models via Ollama). You pick the model you want, and the wrapper handles all the routing automatically. You never need to change anything other than the model name. What Problem Does This Solve? Reading a 30-40 page contract is painful and time-consuming. Important clauses about payment, termination, liability, or IP ownership are often buried deep in legal language. This tool feeds the contract to an AI model and gets back a clean, structured summary in plain English — covering all the sections that matter. How It Works (Plain English)

chunks.title: Open Source LLMs Api Wrapper
chunks.text: ntract to an AI model and gets back a clean, structured summary in plain English — covering all the sections that matter. How It Works (Plain English) This project uses a concept called OpenAI-compatible endpoints. OpenAI invented a standard way to talk to AI models (send a message, get a reply). Other companies — Groq, Google, Mistral — adopted the exact same standard. This means you can use one piece of code to talk to all of them, just by swapping the URL and API key. That is exactly what this wrapper does: The AI model itself reads the full contract text and extracts the key points. The wrapper is just the plumbing that connects you to the right model. chunks.title: Super Resolution Using HAN
chunks.text: # Super Resolution Using HAN Super Resolution using HAN (Holistic Attention Network) architecture Super Resolution using Holistic Attention Network (HAN) Deep Learning Project Developed by: Juvenal F Barajas Shivani Bokka Divya Panchal 📌 Introduction Super-resolution (SR) is the process of reconstructing high-resolution (HR) images from low-resolution (LR) inputs. It restores fine details, sharpens edges, and produces clearer visuals. With the rise of deep learning, SR has seen dramatic improvements in quality and scalability. SR is especially important in domains such as: Medical imaging → Enhancing MRI/CT scans for improved diagnostics. Satellite imaging → Improving clarity for terrain/weather/urban studies. Digital photography → Upscaling images without losing detail. Traditional methods (e.g., bicubic interpolation) fall short, while CNN-based methods (e.g., SRCNN) improved performance but lacked depth. More advanced models like HuSusu and RealFormer improved efficiency but couldn’t fully leverage hierarchical feature relationships. Our project implements and evaluates the Holistic Attention Network (HAN) for super-resolution, with modifications to enhance its performance.

chunks.title: Super Resolution Using HAN
chunks.text: nships. Our project implements and evaluates the Holistic Attention Network (HAN) for super-resolution, with modifications to enhance its performance. 🧠 Why HAN? The HAN architecture introduces hierarchical attention mechanisms that capture both global and local features simultaneously. SRCNN → Simple but limited in feature extraction. HuSusu & RealFormer → Stronger, but less effective at capturing hierarchical dependencies. HAN → Uses attention at multiple levels (layer, channel, spatial), leading to sharper, more precise reconstructions. 🔧 Custom modifications in our implementation: Added an extra convolutional layer for deeper feature extraction. Incorporated a batch normalization layer for stability and improved generalization. 📊 Dataset (DIV2K) We trained on the DIV2K dataset, a gold standard in super-resolution research. 1,000 HR images (2000 px resolution). 800 images used for training, 100 images for validation. Data preparation: Generated 500,000 patches (64×64) for localized learning. Applied rotations, flips for augmentation. Normalized pixel values to [0,1] using Min-Max scaling. Downscaled LR images via bicubic interpolation.

chunks.title: Super Resolution Using HAN
chunks.text: ng. Applied rotations, flips for augmentation. Normalized pixel values to [0,1] using Min-Max scaling. Downscaled LR images via bicubic interpolation. ✅ Advantages: diverse content, high fidelity, scalable for multiple SR factors (×2, ×4, ×8). 🏗️ HAN Model Architecture The HAN integrates multiple attention mechanisms: Layer Attention Module (LAM): Selects outputs from the most relevant layers. Channel Attention Module (CAM): Highlights important feature channels (textures, edges). Spatial Attention Module (SAM): Focuses on key spatial regions (edges, contours). Residual Attention (RA): Learns the difference (residual) between LR and HR, improving detail reconstruction. ➡️ Together, they form a hierarchical attention mechanism enabling robust HR reconstruction. 🧪 Training & Experiments We experimented with different hyperparameter setups: Time Batch Size numcsams tmax Notes 31 hrs 150 12 200 Moderate convergence 28.5 hrs 250 5 50 Rapid loss drop, plateau early 34 hrs 250 5 50 Similar plateau 68.5 hrs 25 12 300 Smooth, stable 157 hrs 45 12 300 Stable, but slow 73.5 hrs 15 15 280 ✅ Best performing configuration

chunks.title: Super Resolution Using HAN
chunks.text: 4 hrs 250 5 50 Similar plateau 68.5 hrs 25 12 300 Smooth, stable 157 hrs 45 12 300 Stable, but slow 73.5 hrs 15 15 280 ✅ Best performing configuration Best configuration: Batch size = 15 numcsams = 15 tmax = 280 Training time = 73.5 hrs 📈 Results Evaluation Metrics: SSIM (Structural Similarity Index): 0.5607 → Moderate structural similarity. PSNR (Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio): 20.44 dB → Reasonable pixel fidelity. Benchmark Comparisons (Urban100, Manga109): Bicubic interpolation: lowest scores. SRCNN: Improved, but limited detail. RCAN, D-DBPN: Strong results with advanced architectures. HAN+ (enhanced): Achieved highest PSNR & SSIM among state-of-the-art. Our HAN implementation: Competitive, but below SOTA, due to training resource limits. 🚀 Future Directions To enhance HAN further: Model refinements: explore dual/adaptive attention, deeper residual learning. Generative AI: integrate diffusion models for sharper, more realistic images. Training improvements: longer training on higher-resolution datasets, multi-scale supervision. New applications: extend to outpainting (content generation beyond boundaries). Optimization: compression for real-time deployment on mobile/IoT devices.

Users complete a short intake survey, sign up, and start logging habits like sleep, water, food, and workouts. A social layer—Wellnest Circle—lets friends create or join group challenges and climb a shared leaderboard.
